match.reason: No existing point teaches continuous improvement; benchmarking, innovation and managing change are related ideas but none covers making many small, staff-driven improvements over time.

draft.title: Continuous improvement
card: Continuous improvement means making many small changes to how work is done, again and again over time. The aim is steady gains in quality, speed or cost.
Ideas often come from the staff who do the work each day. They see where time is lost, where mistakes happen and what could be done more simply.
Small changes are cheap and quick to try. If one does not work, it is easy to drop, so the risk to the business is low.
This differs from waiting for one big change, such as buying a new production line. The business keeps improving all the time instead.
draft.remember: Many small, steady changes, often from staff, add up to better operations.

a.q: Which action is an example of continuous improvement?
opts: A packer suggests a new box layout, and it is trialled
The owner buys a new factory after five years of planning
The business keeps its methods the same until sales fall
A manager replaces the whole production line in one weekend
a.why: A small change that comes from a worker and is tried quickly fits continuous improvement. Replacing the production line is a big change made all at once, which is the opposite approach.
a.clue: Look for a small change that starts with the person doing the job.

b.q: Dev runs a bakery in Newcastle. Each month he asks his staff for one idea to save time, and he trials the best one. Why is this approach less risky than a large one-off redesign of the kitchen?
opts: Each small change is cheap to trial and easy to reverse
Staff ideas are always better than ideas from managers
It removes the need for any spending on equipment
It guarantees that every change will lift quality
b.why: Small changes cost little and can be dropped if they fail, so a bad idea does little harm. Staff ideas are often useful, but that does not make them always better, and no approach guarantees every change works.
b.clue: Think about what happens if one small idea fails.

a.best: A packer suggests a new box layout, and it is trialled

b.best: Each small change is cheap to trial and easy to reverse

problems.detail: All three wrong options rely on absolutes ('guarantees', 'always', 'removes the need for any'), so the right option is the only plain statement. A student could pick it by spotting the absolutes, without knowing why small changes are low-risk.
